notes.body:
The king's dream is really a diagram of two ladders — one hung in heaven, one planted on earth — and the sleep-vision can only show them the way the outward always shows things: in shapes that must be read inward.

The seven lean cows are the seven **speaking prophets** (النُّطَقَاء), each one sent with a new law for humankind:

1. Adam
2. Noah
3. Abraham
4. Moses
5. Jesus
6. Muhammad
7. the awaited one (القَائِم) who completes the cycle

They are called lean because they are driven by need — each hungers upward for what descends from Allah through the ranks above him.

The seven green ears carry a second pairing. Beside each speaker stands a **guardian** (وَلِيّ), the foundation (أَسَاس) who keeps and unfolds what the speaker uttered. In the line we know best, the guardian set beside Muhammad is Maulana Ali, the most trustworthy handhold named earlier in this very conversation.

So how does a cause (سبب) differ from a speaker, when the passage says both stand between Allah and His creation? A cause is the higher, celestial rank — the fat cow that never thins — the unbroken channel of light pouring down from the divine side. The speaker is its earthly mouth: he receives that light and **turns it into human speech and law**, exactly as الْحَوْل, the Imam, turns the Creator's speech into the words of the children of Adam. The cause gives; the speaker voices.

That is why the lean cows eat the fat and the dry ears feed on the green — the earthly rank lives only by drawing on the heavenly one set above it, grace falling ladder-rung by ladder-rung and never once running dry from the hand that sends it.
notes.anchor: they are the seven appointed speakers
notes.quote: they are the seven appointed speakers
etymology: سبب (cause): from the root س-ب-ب, whose oldest sense is the rope let down into a well to draw up water. A سبب is thus a link or means that ties a lower thing to a higher source — so a celestial cause is literally the cord by which grace is drawn down to those below.

نَاطِق (speaker): from the root ن-ط-ق, to speak or give utterance. A نَاطِق is the one who voices — the prophet who takes the silent inner light and gives it audible body as speech and law, so what was hidden becomes something people can hear and follow.

وَلِيّ (guardian): from the root و-ل-ي, to be near, to stand next to, to take charge of. A وَلِيّ is one who stands closest and holds guardianship — hence the friend of Allah set nearest the speaker, keeping and interpreting what was given.

أَسَاس (foundation): from the root أ-س-س, to lay a base or footing. An أَسَاس is the groundwork a building rests on — so the guardian is called this because the whole structure of a prophet's law stands firm only upon the one who carries and secures its inner meaning.

notes.body:
The Master answers the boy's question by refusing to answer it flatly, and that refusal is itself the teaching. He has given the boy a ladder, not a single object, and a ladder is climbed rung by rung, not described from the ground. What the boy can hold in his hand today is the one who stands before him — his guide, the door to the Imam, whom the Master calls his rope and his most trustworthy handhold (الْعُرْوَة الْوُثْقَى). Above that guide is the Imam, and the Imam is not the rope itself but its **outward sign**, the visible knot of a cord whose far end is anchored out of sight.

The whole image is drawn from a single command:
وَاعْتَصِمُوا بِحَبْلِ اللَّهِ جَمِيعًا
Hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah.
Al Imran 3:103

Read the Master's own words closely — he says the seeker is guided *by a rope from Allah* (حَبْل مِنَ اللَّهِ) *to the rope of Allah* (حَبْل اللَّهِ). Those are not two cords but the two ends of one, and the difference between them is direction:

- The rope that comes from Allah is guidance let *down* — the living chain of the Imam, his proof, and his callers, lowered toward us so that a person on the ground has something real to grasp.
- The rope of Allah is that same cord seen at its *upper* anchor, tied fast in the divine world where it begins, which is why the Master calls it the end of the boy's guidance and the utmost of the worlds.

So the seeker climbs from the rope that reaches him to the rope where it is fastened. The Master will not name the far end plainly because **it is a station arrived at, never merely heard**. To describe it would be to hand the boy an outward word for an inward place; the word would be true and still leave him standing exactly where he was. The only way to know what the cord is tied to is to climb it.
notes.anchor: That is the end of your guidance and the utmost of the worlds
notes.quote: That is the end of your guidance and the utmost of the worlds
etymology: حَبْل (rope, cord): from the root ح-ب-ل, the sense of binding and tying fast. The same root gives the cord one draws water with and the bond of a covenant, so a rope in this language is never dead fibre but a live tie between two parties — which is why guidance itself can be called a rope: it binds the one below to the one above.

الْعُرْوَة الْوُثْقَى (the most trustworthy handhold): عُرْوَة, from ع-ر-و, is the loop or handle of a vessel, the part made precisely to be gripped; وُثْقَى, from و-ث-ق, means firmly bound and reliable. Together, the one handhold that will not tear away when the whole weight of a person hangs from it — Al-Baqarah 2:256.

الْحُجَّة (proof, the one who establishes the argument): from ح-ج-ج, to make for a goal and to argue with a decisive case. The root also gives the pilgrimage (حَجّ), a journey toward a fixed destination, so the حُجَّة is at once the standing evidence of the Imam and the appointed way one travels toward him.

notes.body:
Think of a single year and how it turns. It is one whole thing, yet completed only across twelve months, and no month stands alone — each carries the year forward until it comes full circle. The speaking Imam is called the اَلْحَوْل, the year, for the same reason: he is one, yet **his light reaches creation only through twelve who complete him**.

Those twelve are the captains, the نُقَبَاء — also named the twelve حُجَج and, together, the عُصْبَة, the band of men "possessed of power." They are not rivals to the Imam and not copies of him. They are the vessels through which his single voice is carried outward, the way twelve months carry the one year.

Beside the Imam stands one who is foremost among these twelve, and he is the قُوَّة, the strength. He is the Imam's own حُجَّة and his door: **he receives the Creator's speech from the Imam in summary and hands it down, in detail, to the callers** (الدُّعَاة), each taking his share according to his place. So the burden of utterance is borne in ranks — from the Imam, to his door, to the twelve, to the callers, and then to the people.

The Master reads all of this into Joseph's dream, where Joseph sees the sun, the moon, and eleven planets:

يَا أَبَتِ إني رأيْتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَباً وَالشَّمْسَ وَالقَمَرَ رَأَيْتُهُمْ لِي سَاجِدِيْنَ
O my father, I saw eleven planets, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.
Yusuf 12:4

The sun is the Imam; the moon is his حُجَّة and his door, the قُوَّة; and the eleven planets, joined to the moon, complete the twelve captains. So the one strengthened at the Imam's side is himself the first of the twelve — nearest and brightest, as the moon is nearest among the lights of the night.
notes.anchor: the lord of the twelve captains
notes.quote: the lord of the twelve captains
etymology: حَوْل (year): from the root ح-و-ل, to turn, shift, or come full circle. A year is a حَوْل because time turns and returns to where it began; the Imam bears the same name because he turns (يحوّل) the hidden speech of the Creator into the plain speech of people — the very same turning.

قُوَّة (power): from the root ق-و-ي, to be strong. It names the حُجَّة who stands beside the Imam because Allah has strengthened him alone to carry the heavy weight of utterance and pass it on — strength given, not owned.

نَقِيب (captain): from the root ن-ق-ب, to bore through or search out. A نَقِيب is a chief who sees into the affairs and the inner state of those under him and vouches for them — a leader knit to his people, not set above them.

حُجَّة (proof): from the root ح-ج-ج, to argue decisively and to aim toward a goal. A حُجَّة is the clinching proof; here it is the man through whom Allah establishes His own argument (حُجَّة) upon creation.

عُصْبَة (band): from the root ع-ص-ب, to bind tightly, as a sinew or nerve (عَصَب) binds the body. A عُصْبَة is a group knit close together by kinship — here the twelve حُجَج bound around the one Imam.

دُعَاة (callers): from the root د-ع-و, to call or summon. A داعي (plural دُعَاة) is one who calls people onward — the caller who summons to the Imam and hands down, in detail, the teaching he receives.
